claims.text: The target material is a Mg-containing, Mg-Ti-Zn-based lightweight high-entropy or multi-principal-element alloy.
Bulk Mg-Ti-Zn alloys can be produced by powder metallurgy using ball milling and spark plasma sintering.
The as-fabricated alloy has a metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution-containing microstructure.
The proposed intervention is 50-100 rapid thermal cycles between approximately 25°C and 500°C with peak holds of a few minutes.
Using an inert or controlled-oxygen atmosphere will limit extraneous oxidation during cycling and permit comparison with a non-cycled control.
Repeated rapid thermal cycling generates localized transient temperature gradients and cyclic thermal stresses in the alloy.
The transient gradients generated by cycling enhance local atomic mobility, particularly Mg diffusion.
Enhanced Mg diffusion promotes heterogeneous nucleation and growth of intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-Ti-Zn alloys have a tendency to form stable intermetallic compounds, including Ti2Zn and TiZn16.
Intermetallic spatial distribution, morphology, and size are important determinants of corrosion performance in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys.
Intermetallic phases can provide corrosion shielding but can also accelerate localized Mg dissolution through micro-galvanic coupling.
Evolution of intermetallic precipitate morphology affects the formation and maintenance of protective surface passivation layers.
Changes in passivation-layer integrity control both aqueous corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Relative to the initial state, thermal cycling will produce a refined dispersion of intermetallic precipitates and change their size distribution and volume fraction.
The cycling-induced precipitate changes will correlate with measurable changes in corrosion current, passivation behavior, oxidation kinetics, and oxide thickness.
A critical cycle count or thermal intensity separates a beneficial precipitate-refinement regime from a deleterious coarsening regime.
The magnitude and direction of the corrosion and oxidation response may vary with processing and environmental conditions.

The hypothesis is falsified if cycling produces neither a statistically significant or model-consistent precipitate change nor a corrosion or oxidation change beyond experimental uncertainty relative to the control.
